Citation: Andersen RM. Revisiting the behavioral model and access to medical care: does it matter?
Key finding / contribution: Reviews the development and continued relevance of the Behavioral Model of Health Services Use.
Relevance to this project: Primary conceptual basis for predisposing, enabling, and need factors.
Caution / limitation: Conceptual framework; does not establish causal effects for this NHIS outcome.

Citation: Babitsch B, Gohl D, von Lengerke T. Re-revisiting Andersen's Behavioral Model of Health Services Use: a systematic review of studies from 1998–2011.
Key finding / contribution: Common operationalizations included age, sex, education, ethnicity, income, insurance, and health status; implementations varied.
Caution / limitation: Not specific to cost-related unmet care; operationalizations varied substantially.

Citation: Braveman P, Gottlieb L. The social determinants of health: it's time to consider the causes of the causes.
Key finding / contribution: Emphasizes upstream social and economic conditions in health and health inequities.
Relevance to this project: Supports SDOH framing for poverty, education, employment, food security, and social context.
Caution / limitation: Broad SDOH paper; not an NHIS prediction study.

Citation: Alemu FW et al. Social determinants of unmet need for primary care: a systematic review.
Key finding / contribution: Socioeconomic, mental-health, and chronic-condition factors recur, with heterogeneous demographic patterns.
Relevance to this project: Supports SDOH and need variables while anticipating subgroup heterogeneity.
Caution / limitation: Unmet primary care broadly, not specifically NHIS 2024 cost-related unmet care.

Citation: Mahajan S et al. Trends in Differences in Health Status and Health Care Access and Affordability by Race and Ethnicity in the United States, 1999–2018.
Key finding / contribution: Documents persistent racial/ethnic differences in health status, access, and affordability measures.
Relevance to this project: Justifies subgroup/equity evaluation and social/structural interpretation.
Caution / limitation: Descriptive/association study; not ML fairness analysis and predates NHIS 2024.

Citation: Cai J, Bidulescu A. Trends in unmet health care needs among adults in the U.S., 2019–2021.
Study design / method: Cross-sectional trend analysis with survey weighting
Key finding / contribution: Cost-related unmet-care prevalence changed over time and differed across socioeconomic groups.
Relevance to this project: Directly supports outcome relevance and national NHIS context.

Citation: Casagrande SS, Lawrence JM. Trends in delaying and forgoing medical care due to cost and the association with insurance status among US adults with diabetes, 2009–2023.
Key finding / contribution: Delayed/forgone care due to cost varied by insurance, income, education, race/ethnicity, and age.
Relevance to this project: Closely aligned NHIS cost-related outcomes; reinforces insurance/SES relevance.
Caution / limitation: Restricted to adults with diabetes; not general adult ML/XAI/fairness.
Use in paper: Related Work / Closest NHIS outcome study

Citation: Azubuike CD, Alawode OA. Delayed Healthcare Due to Cost Among Adults with Multimorbidity in the United States.
Population / Data: U.S. adults with multimorbidity; NHIS 2016–2018 and 2020–2021
Key finding / contribution: Examines cost-related delayed healthcare among adults with multiple chronic conditions and socioeconomic characteristics.
Relevance to this project: Supports a chronic-condition burden construct instead of only one or two diseases.
Caution / limitation: Restricted to multimorbidity population and delayed-care outcome.

Citation: Berkowitz SA, Seligman HK, Choudhry NK. Treat or Eat: Food Insecurity, Cost-related Medication Underuse, and Unmet Needs.
Population / Data: Nationally representative U.S. adults with chronic disease
Key finding / contribution: Food insecurity was linked with cost-related medication underuse and competing material needs.
Relevance to this project: Supports food insecurity as a material-hardship construct relevant to affordability.
Caution / limitation: Medication underuse is not identical to forgone medical care.

Citation: Bertoldo J et al. Food Insecurity and Delayed or Forgone Medical Care During the COVID-19 Pandemic.
Key finding / contribution: Food insecurity was associated with delaying or forgoing medical care because of cost concerns.
Relevance to this project: Direct support for food security as a predictor of cost-related care barriers.
Caution / limitation: Pandemic-period context may differ from NHIS 2024.

Citation: Cole MB, Nguyen KH. Unmet social needs among low-income adults in the United States: Associations with health care access and quality.
Population / Data: 2017 BRFSS SDOH module, 12 U.S. states, low-income adults
Key finding / contribution: Greater unmet social needs were associated with poorer access, including inability to see a doctor because of cost.
Relevance to this project: Supports multidimensional SDOH interpretation beyond income alone.
Caution / limitation: Not nationally representative of all U.S. adults and not NHIS.

Citation: MacNell N et al. Implementing machine learning methods with complex survey data: Lessons learned on the impacts of accounting sampling weights in gradient boosting.
Key finding / contribution: Accounting for sampling weights can materially affect gradient-boosting modeling and interpretation.
Relevance to this project: Direct rationale for conventional vs survey-weighted ML comparison.
Caution / limitation: Survey weights alone do not reproduce all aspects of full design-based inference.

Citation: Dey D et al. The proper application of logistic regression model in complex survey data: a systematic review.
Key finding / contribution: Finds frequent shortcomings in handling survey design, missing information, validation, and diagnostics.
Relevance to this project: Supports explicit reporting of weighting/design limits, missing handling, and validation.
Caution / limitation: Evidence base is DHS/MICS rather than NHIS; LR-focused.

Citation: Matabuena M, Vidal JC, Ghosal R, Onnela JP. Screening for diabetes mellitus in the US population using neural network-based modeling and complex survey designs.
Key finding / contribution: Develops predictive modeling that explicitly incorporates complex-survey information.
Relevance to this project: Shows survey-aware ML is active and methodologically nontrivial.
Caution / limitation: Different outcome/model; current project does not claim to implement their full method.

Citation: Loh HW et al. Application of explainable artificial intelligence for healthcare: A systematic review of the last decade (2011–2022).
Key finding / contribution: Reviews XAI applications and interpretability needs in healthcare predictive systems.
Relevance to this project: Supports SHAP as an explainability layer while separating prediction from causation.
Caution / limitation: Broad review; does not validate SHAP as causal inference.

Citation: Sun F et al. Social Determinants, Cardiovascular Disease, and Health Care Cost: A Nationwide Study in the United States Using Machine Learning.
Key finding / contribution: Shows ML can integrate SDOH information for health and cost-related analysis at population scale.
Relevance to this project: Precedent for SDOH-informed ML; using ML+SDOH is not itself novel.

Citation: Wang RC, Sambamoorthi U. Predicting Anticipated Telehealth Use: Development of the CONTEST Score and Machine Learning Models Using a National U.S. Survey.
Key finding / contribution: Combines national survey data with regression/ML approaches for a health-services outcome.
Relevance to this project: Recent precedent for national-survey weighting and multiple ML models.
Caution / limitation: Different outcome/survey; not cost-related unmet care.

Citation: Rajkomar A, Hardt M, Howell MD, Corrado G, Chin MH. Ensuring Fairness in Machine Learning to Advance Health Equity.
Key finding / contribution: Describes ways ML systems can reproduce disparities and motivates explicit group-level evaluation.
Relevance to this project: Supports subgroup performance auditing and cautious fairness interpretation.
Caution / limitation: Conceptual/methodological paper, not an empirical NHIS fairness study.
